Maladaptive Strategies.value: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
I have lost my connection to my community and culture
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

vignette:
Mai Lee was twenty years old, a soldier, and she had been married for just over a year when the assault happened. She was stationed at a large base in the southern United States, a place where the heat felt thick and the days were long. The assault occurred in the barracks, late one evening, after a training exercise that had left everyone exhausted. A fellow soldier, someone she had considered a friend, cornered her in the laundry room. She remembered the fluorescent lights, the smell of detergent and bleach, the way the concrete floor felt cold through her boots. She did not scream, because she had been trained not to make noise in close quarters. She froze, and it was over in minutes. In the weeks that followed, she told no one. She was certain that someone else—anyone else—would have stopped it. A stronger person, a louder person, a person who had not been raised to be quiet and polite, would have shoved him away, would have made a scene. She replayed the moment endlessly, trying to find the exact point where she could have acted differently, but the images were all she had: the flickering light, the pattern on his uniform, the way the dryer hummed. They came to her as snapshots, not as a story she could tell. The memory felt alien, as if it had happened to a different woman, a weaker woman, and Mai Lee could not connect that woman to herself. The event itself was so extreme, so far outside anything she had ever imagined, that she sometimes doubted it had happened at all. She would lie in bed next to her husband, staring at the ceiling, and think: *That cannot be my life.*

She began to eat. Not because she was hungry, but because the act of chewing, of tasting, of filling her mouth with something other than the words she could not say, gave her a few minutes of relief. She would buy fast food on her way back to the base, eat it in her car, and then throw the wrappers away before she went inside. At night, she would stand in front of the open refrigerator, eating spoonfuls of peanut butter or cold rice, until her stomach hurt. When the images came—and they came most often in the quiet moments, during guard duty or while she was trying to fall asleep—she learned to redirect her mind. She would think about her mother’s kitchen, the smell of lemongrass and fish sauce, the sound of her grandmother’s voice. She would count the tiles on the ceiling, or recite the names of every drill instructor she had ever had. But the redirection only worked for a few seconds, and then the images came back, and she would start the process all over again. She also overanalysed. She went over the details of the event again and again, trying to make sense of it, trying to find a logic that would explain why it had happened to her. She examined her own behaviour like a piece of faulty equipment: *I should have seen it coming. I should have walked the other way. I should have said something. I should have been someone else.*

The person she had become was unrecognisable to her. Before the assault, Mai Lee had been proud of her place in the military. She had felt strong, capable, part of something larger than herself. Now, she felt disconnected from everything that had once defined her. She had lost her connection to her community and culture. The other Southeast Asian soldiers on base, the ones she used to share meals and jokes with, now seemed like strangers. She stopped going to the gatherings, the potlucks, the celebrations. She told herself they would not understand, that they would see her as weak, that she had brought shame on her family. Her husband noticed the change. He asked her what was wrong, and she told him she was tired, that the training was hard, that she was just stressed. He believed her, because he wanted to, and because she had always been good at hiding things. But the hiding made her feel even more alone. She was surrounded by people who saw a soldier, a wife, a friend, and inside she was a stranger.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment on the firing range. She was qualifying with her rifle, and the sound of the shots—sharp, percussive, echoing—sent her into a state she could not name. Her hands shook. Her vision narrowed. She dropped to her knees and pressed her palms flat against the hot ground, trying to anchor herself to something real. Her sergeant asked if she was okay, and for the first time, she said no. She was terrified of what would happen next. She was afraid of being seen as broken, of being discharged, of losing the only identity she had left. But she was also afraid of staying the same. She wanted to feel like herself again, even if she no longer knew who that was. She wanted the memory to feel like her own. She wanted to stop eating in the dark. She wanted to believe that the person she had been was still inside her, somewhere, waiting to be found.
